Returning the tensor hands back a tensor object, not a list. The block has to be converted back to plain Python before it is returned.

`==` compares elementwise and returns a tensor of bools. The question asks for ONE verdict about the whole tensor, not a verdict per element.

wrong_examples.why: Pulling a Python number out of a tensor only works when it holds exactly one element. Without checking the element count first, a two-element input raises instead of returning None.
`==` is elementwise and returns a tensor of bools. The first slot asks for a single True/False verdict about the whole tensor.
The third answer is asked about the PACKED copy, not the view. Reusing the view means the third answer is still the view's.
The last slot is the ELEMENT count, not the axis count.
`len()` is the first axis only. The third slot asks for the total number of elements.
The packed copy is a NEW tensor with its own block, in reading order. Reusing the view instead of packing it leaves three of the four answers wrong.
Indexing gives a 0-d tensor. The middle slot asks for the plain Python number stored in it.
The first slot rounds DOWN and the second rounds UP; returning them in the other order reports each one in the wrong slot.
The third slot hands back a function object instead of the number it computes — the parentheses are what make it a call.
The prompt fixes the COLUMN count, which is the last axis — so the -1 goes first. Putting the fixed count first fixes the row count instead.
full puts v in every cell. The question asks for v on the diagonal ONLY, with zeros everywhere else — the identity, scaled by v.
argsort answers WHERE the sorted values came from — indices, not values. The first two slots ask for the sorted values themselves.
The first row asked for is the TRANSPOSE's — column 0 of a. Taking row 0 of a itself hands back a's own first row.
The size arguments are read in order: the first is the number of rows, the second the number of columns. Swapping them transposes the shape you asked for.
Drawing random integers samples WITH replacement, so it repeats values and skips others. The question asks for a shuffling: every number 0..n-1 appears exactly once.
An unseeded generator starts from a nondeterministic state, so passing the same seed argument no longer replays the same numbers — the seed has to be applied to the generator itself.
